opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I've been at Google for close to ten years now, and the culture has changed quite a lot over that time.

When I joined Google Brain, robotics was a small, exploratory effort. It felt like an academic lab inside a big company. Researchers had a lot of freedom to pick their own problems, and many projects were bottom-up. I came from computer graphics and physics-based simulation, so I worked on simulation and sim-to-real transfer for legged robots. I'd train a locomotion policy in simulation, put it on a small quadruped, and see whether it could walk. The teams were small, the goals were specific, and we measured success with papers and demos.

Then a few things changed the culture. The first was scale. After large language models took off, we saw that general-purpose models trained on huge amounts of data could beat many hand-designed, task-specific systems. Robotics started asking the same question: could we build a foundation model for robots instead of one policy per task? That changed how we work. Projects became bigger and more collaborative, with dozens of people working toward one shared model instead of each researcher owning a small project.

The second was the merger of Brain and DeepMind. The two groups had different styles. Brain was more open and bottom-up, and DeepMind was more mission-driven and organized around big goals. The combined culture is more focused. There's a clearer sense of which directions matter most, and more willingness to put serious resources behind them.

The third is that robotics now builds directly on the frontier models. We used to build perception, planning, and control mostly from scratch. Now a lot of our work starts from very capable multimodal models that already understand images, language, and much of common-sense knowledge about the world. The question has become how to ground that knowledge in the physical world, so that a robot can turn understanding into reliable action.

Some things haven't changed, and I hope they never do. People still care a lot about rigor and about testing ideas on real hardware, because the real world is unforgiving. A demo that works in simulation, or works once on video, is very different from a robot that works robustly every day. That respect for the physical world has always been at the core of the robotics team.

Overall, we've moved from many small, curiosity-driven bets to a more concentrated effort toward general-purpose embodied intelligence. That has trade-offs, but for the first time I feel like the goal of a truly capable, general robot is within sight, and that's very exciting.

r001.rationale: It says researchers had “a lot of freedom to pick their own problems” when robotics was a small effort.

r002.rationale: It describes the early teams as small, but does not connect their size to easier resource allocation.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because I've been at Google for quite a long time now, and the culture has really gone through a few distinct phases.

When I first joined, Google Brain was still relatively small, and the robotics effort was almost a side project. There was a lot of freedom. You could pick a problem that you personally found interesting, spend months on it, publish a paper, and nobody would really ask you how it connected to a product. The emphasis was on curiosity and on being first to show that something was possible. For robotics, that meant a lot of work on reinforcement learning, sim-to-real transfer, legged locomotion, those kinds of fundamental questions. It felt very much like an academic lab with much better compute.

Then, over the years, two things changed. One was scale. Once large models started working, the whole organization realized that the biggest wins came from very large, coordinated efforts rather than many small independent ones. That naturally pushes the culture toward bigger teams, shared infrastructure, and more alignment on a few central bets. The other change was the merger of Brain and DeepMind into Google DeepMind. That brought together two cultures that were actually quite different. DeepMind had a longer tradition of mission-driven, top-down programs, while Brain was more bottom-up. Merging them required a lot of adjustment on both sides.

For robotics specifically, I think the shift has been from "can we make this work in a lab" to "can we build a general robot foundation model." That's a much more ambitious goal, and it requires much tighter collaboration between the people who collect data, the people who train models, and the people who maintain the robots. So the culture is less about the individual researcher's project and more about the collective system.

I have mixed feelings, honestly. I do miss some of the early freedom, and I think it's important that there's still room for exploration, because many of the ideas that power today's systems came from that era. But I also see that the larger, more focused approach is producing things that simply weren't possible before. Robots that can follow natural language instructions, that generalize across tasks, that's something I dreamed about when I joined and didn't think I would see this quickly.

So I'd say the culture has become more disciplined and more product-aware, but the underlying ambition, which is to really solve intelligence and embodiment, has actually gotten stronger, not weaker.

r001.rationale: The response says there was a lot of freedom to pick a personally interesting problem and work on it.

r002.rationale: It says Google Brain was relatively small, but does not connect that size to easier resource allocation.

astra-6.text:
The biggest change I’ve felt is a growing emphasis on bringing research into real-world applications. When I joined, there was more room to explore an idea primarily because it was scientifically interesting. That freedom still matters, but now we also ask much earlier: What can this enable? Can it work reliably outside the lab?

In robotics, that shift is particularly challenging. A promising result in simulation or a controlled experiment is only the beginning. Getting a robot to handle variation in the real world requires a lot of work that doesn’t necessarily look like a new research breakthrough.

There’s also a stronger connection between robotics and the broader progress in AI. We’re thinking less about solving each robot task in isolation and more about how learning and knowledge can transfer across tasks. For me, that makes this a very exciting period, although it also means balancing the urgency to build useful systems with the patience that robotics research requires.

r001.rationale: The candidate says there was more room to explore ideas for scientific interest, but does not state that researchers could choose their own work.

r002.rationale: It does not mention resource allocation or connect its ease to the early robotics team's small size.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change is how closely AI and robotics are connected now. When I joined, robotics often meant building a system for a very specific task, with a lot of specialized engineering. Increasingly, the question is how we can build more general capabilities—how a robot can learn from different tasks and transfer what it has learned to a new situation.

That also changes the research culture. People working on robotics, machine learning, and language models have more reasons to collaborate. There’s a stronger emphasis on bringing ideas together and seeing whether they work on a real robot.

But robotics still has its own rhythm. You can make progress very quickly in software, while a physical robot forces you to deal with reliability, safety, and the complexity of the real world. For me, the exciting part is bringing that ambition in AI together with the discipline of making something actually work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a shift toward general capabilities and cross-disciplinary collaboration, but does not say researchers initially had autonomy to choose their own work.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention the early robotics team’s size or connect team size to how easily resources were allocated.
